children.text: You can make words and numbers move across the LED display of the Calliope mini. Show a string of your choice, followed by a number.
The function scrolls a text and value horizontally on the display.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *


display.scroll('Emma is: ')    
display.scroll(16)

children.text: The value can be an integer, float (decimal), or string. The speed of the scrolling is controlled by the delay parameter, with a default delay of 150ms if not specified explicitly.
Enhance scrolling functionality by incorporating additional options:
If
wait
is set to
True
, the function will wait until the scrolling animation is complete before continuing.
If
wait
is set to
False
, the animation will occur asynchronously in the background.
Setting
loop
to
True
will cause the animation to repeat indefinitely.
When
monospace
is True, each character will occupy 5 pixel-columns in width; otherwise, there will be exactly 1 blank pixel-column between each scrolling character.
For instance, the following code continuously scrolls the word 'Emma' at an accelerated pace in a loop, while simultaneously lighting the RGB-LED:

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel


display.scroll('Emma', delay=200, wait=True, loop=True, monospace=False)

np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, 3)
np[0] = (255, 0, 0)
np[1] = (0, 128, 0)
np[2] = (0, 0, 64)
np.show()

children.text: In Python, indentations delineate which instructions are part of a loop or outside of it.
Indentation needs to be consistent, since python uses indentation to block code together.
This loop for example scrolls 'Emma' on the LED display two times. The Calliope mini Python editor automatically adds indentations when you press 'enter' after typing
for i in range(2):

. It's crucial to maintain consistent spacing, typically using 4 spaces or a tab, for clear code readability. Incorrect indentation will be flagged by the editor. Use the tab key to indent a line and press shift+tab to remove indentations.
To run a program infinitely, a while or 'forever' loop can be created, if the condition is permanently true. 'Emma' will perpetually scroll across the LED display:
The
while loop
is a prevalent technique for ongoing monitoring of inputs, such as sensor readings:
Make the code take a break using the sleep function:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

while True:
    display.scroll('Emma')
    sleep(1500)

children.text: Turn off all the lights on the LED display by using
clear

content.main:
from calliopemini import *


display.clear()

children.text: You can fill out all RGB LEDs with the fill function:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel

n = 3
np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, n)

np.fill((255,0,0)) # fills all pixel with the color red
np.show()

children.text: Don't forget to call the function
np.show()
afterwards!
You will find more information on RGB LEDs within the
RGB LED reference
in the Toolkit.

children.text: Use built-in buttons and sensors with concise coding insights. Elevate your ideas by unlocking practical input possibilities.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

while True:
    if button_a.is_pressed() and button_b.is_pressed():
        display.set_pixel(4, 2, 9)
        display.set_pixel(0, 2, 9)
        sleep(1500)
        display.clear()

from calliopemini import *

while True:
    if button_a.is_pressed() or button_b.is_pressed():
        display.set_pixel(2,2,9)
        display.set_pixel(2,4,9)
        sleep(1500)
        display.clear()

children.text: Employ
is_pressed()
to determine if a button is currently being pressed. In the given example, LEDs will light up depending on what button/buttons are pressed.

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
while True:
    if button_a.is_pressed() and button_b.is_pressed():
        display.set_pixel(4, 2, 9)
        display.set_pixel(0, 2, 9)
        sleep(1500)
        display.clear()
    elif button_a.is_pressed():
        display.set_pixel(0, 2, 9)
        sleep(1500)
        display.clear()
    elif button_b.is_pressed():
        display.set_pixel(4, 2, 9)
        sleep(1500)
        display.clear()
    sleep(200)

children.text: Ensure also to check if buttons A and B are pressed simultaneously, as opposed to separate checks for each button. This approach is essential to accurately capture the scenario where both buttons are pressed at the same time.
Pins P0, P1, P2, and P3 can also function as touch sensors when you touch the minus (GND) pin, completing an electrical circuit:
The Calliope mini V3 has a gold logo on the back that you can use as an extra button when you touch it:
By default, pins operate in resistive touch mode, necessitating touch on both the pin and GND. For Calliope mini V3, you have the option to switch to
capacitive
mode, requiring only a touch without GND. This configuration is already the default state on the touch-logo pin.

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin1.set_touch_mode(pin1.CAPACITIVE)

children.text: To revert this to
resistive
touch, you can define a pin like this:

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin1.set_touch_mode(pin1.RESISTIVE)

children.text: You can use gestures in your program to detect when your Calliope mini is moved in different ways.
Triggered when you shake your Calliope mini:
Triggered when the Calliope mini is upright with the logo at the top:
Triggered when the Calliope mini is upside down with the logo at the bottom:
Triggered when the Calliope mini is lying flat with the LED display facing up:
Triggered when your Calliope mini is lying flat with its LED display facing down:
Triggered when the Calliope mini is tilted left or held upright with the logo on the left:
Triggered when the Calliope mini is tilted right or held upright with the logo on the right:
Triggered when the accelerometer detects it's falling towards the ground:
Triggered when the accelerometer detects acceleration of around 3g:
1g equals gravity's pull, while 3g and beyond very fast movement, like a speed roller coaster, so generating accelerations above 3g in a classroom is challenging.
Employ
was_gesture
to detect any gesture since the last test, and
is_gesture
to check if a gesture is currently active.
The LEDs on the Calliope mini can also act as a light sensor:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.scroll(display.read_light_level())

children.text: The intensity of light incident on the Calliope mini is gauged on a scale from 0 to 255, where 0 represents the darkest and 255 the brightest.
The following code illuminates one pixel in the middle of the LED display when the light level drops below 50:

Because the temperature sensor is integrated into the processor, the temperature can slightly increase during high processor load. If you require precise temperature readings, it is advisable to calibrate the values or use an external sensor.
The Calliope mini has a temperature sensor inside its processor. You can take temperature readings in centigrade like this:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.scroll(temperature())

children.text: The accelerometer is capable of gauging the intensity of acceleration across three dimensions: x, y, and z.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

x = accelerometer.get_x()
display.scroll(x)

from calliopemini import *

y = accelerometer.get_y()
display.scroll(y)

from calliopemini import *

z = accelerometer.get_z()
display.scroll(z)

children.text: The Calliope mini quantifies acceleration in milli-g units (mg), equivalent to one-thousandth of Earth's gravitational force.
When the Calliope mini is placed flat on a table, the x and y values are approximately 0, while the z value is around -1000, indicating the accelerometer's measurement of gravity.
The accelerometer's readings range from a minimum of -2000 to a maximum of +2000 milli-g.
The microphone can detect sound levels ranging from 0 to 255, with 0 indicating the lowest (quietest) level and 255 indicating the highest (loudest) level.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.scroll(microphone.sound_level())

children.text: You can also display the volume graphically with a short code:
The Calliope mini has a built-in an e-compass that can measure its heading or bearing in degrees relative to magnetic North.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *


display.scroll(compass.heading())

children.text: You can also recreate a traditional compass by assigning the values to the directions.

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *

# Function to determine compass direction based on heading
def get_compass_direction(heading):
    directions = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW", "N"]
    index = int((heading + 22.5) / 45) % 8
    return directions[index]

while True:
    # Get current compass heading
    current_heading = compass.heading()

    # Determine compass direction
    current_direction = get_compass_direction(current_heading)

    # Display compass direction and heading
    display.show(current_direction)
    sleep(1000)  # Update display every 1 second

children.text: When using the compass for the first time, you might be prompted to  calibrate it through a brief game. The message 'TILT TO FILL SCREEN' will scroll across the display. Tilt the Calliope mini until all LED lights are lit, and a happy face will appear.

The compass on the Calliope mini can function as a magnetometer, allowing you to measure the strength of magnetic fields. It is capable of measuring magnetic field strength in three dimensions and can also provide an overall measurement of magnetic field strength across all dimensions simultaneously.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

magnet_strength_x = compass.get_x()
display.scroll(magnet_strength_x)

from calliopemini import *

magnet_strength_y = compass.get_y()
display.scroll(magnet_strength_y)

from calliopemini import *

magnet_strength_z = compass.get_z()
display.scroll(magnet_strength_z)

from calliopemini import *

magnet_strength_all = compass.get_field_strength()
display.scroll(magnet_strength_all)

children.text: Magnetic field strength is measured by the compass in units known as nanoteslas (nT). The readings may be positive or negative based on the orientation of the magnetic field.

contents.subtitle: The Calliope mini uses its LED display to show information or images.

children.text: You can display words and numbers character by character:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.show('Calliope mini is: ')
sleep(500)
display.show(7)
sleep(2000)
display.clear()

children.text: You can incorporate optional parameters such as
delay
loop
, and
wait
The
delay
parameter regulates the speed at which multiple characters, digits, or images appear. A
delay
below 400ms speeds up the display, while anything above 400ms slows it down.
If the
loop
parameter is set to
True
, the show function will continuously loop. Its default value is
False
, indicating no looping.
The
wait
parameter determines the duration of the program's pause before executing the next instruction.
In the following example, a countdown will be continuously displayed in a loop with a 1-second interval between each number, and there will be no wait before executing the next instruction:

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.show(12345, delay=200, loop=True, wait=False)

children.text: You can create images with depth by assigning individual brightness values to each LED. The brightness of each LED is indicated by a number ranging from 0 (off) to 9 (brightest):

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.show(Image('00000:'
                   '33333:'
                   '55555:'
                   '77777:'
                   '99999'))

children.text: This example illustrates a transition that is vivid at the upper edge and gradually diminishes towards the lower edge of the LED display.

A pixel represents a single point in an image. Every LED serves as a pixel within a Calliope mini image. Each pixel is identified by its x and y coordinates, commencing from the upper left corner with 0,0.

Utilize numbers ranging from 0 to 9 to designate the brightness level for each pixel, where 9 represents the brightest. The following code snippet in Python will illuminate the top-left LED at its maximum brightness:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.set_pixel(0,0,9)

children.text: You can determine the brightness of a pixel. The following code will read the brightness of the top-right pixel and store a value between 0 and 9 in a variable named
top:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
 top = display.get_pixel(4,4)

children.text: This program will populate the LED display incrementally, one pixel at a time:
Note that this employs a nested
loop
, which consists of a loop within another loop.

contents.name: LED

contents.subtitle: Use the RGB LEDs to show different colors

children.text: The calliope mini has three integrated rgb-leds that can represent 256 colors per color channel (red, green, blue), thus able to represent 256^3 = 16 777 216 colors.

The RGB LEDs are so-called neopixels. These are special individually addressable RGB LEDs similar to the individual pixels on a display. With the help of Python's Neopixel module, we can program them and light them up.
First of all you need to import the neopixel module and create a neopixel strip with the pin and amount of 3 as parameters. You can store the Neopixel instance in a variable:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel

np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, 3)

children.text: Set the first LED to red at full brightness, the second LED to green at half brightness and the last LED to blue at quarter brightness:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel

np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, 3)

np[0] = (255, 0, 0) # set first LED to red, full brightness
np[1] = (0, 128, 0) # set second LED to green, half brightness
np[2] = (0, 0, 64)  # set third LED to blue, quarter brightness

np.show()

children.text: To see the effect on the pixel you must always update them with
np.show
You can fill out all RGB LEDs with the fill function:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel

n = 3
np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, n)

np.fill((255,0,0)) # fills all pixel with the color red
np.show()

children.text: Don't forget to call the function
np.show()
afterwards!
The function
fill()
uses a color tuple as a parameter so you need to enclose the three values in to two brackets:
You can select the single RGB LEDs like an item of an array, by their index
np[i]
and also iterate through them in a loop. It has the same effect as fill:

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel


np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, 3)
n = np.n # get the amount of pixels of the neopixel object

    for i in range(n):
        np[i] = (255, 0, 0) # this sets all rgb leds to red
    np.show()

children.text: You can clear all LEDs by calling the function
clear()
. In this example, all LEDs blink red:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel

n = 3
np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, n)

while True:
    np.fill((255,0,0))
    np.show()
    sleep(500)
    np.clear()
    sleep(500)

children.text: When creating color transitions or animations you can change the color values in a loop.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import neopixel

n = 3
np = neopixel.NeoPixel(pin_RGB, n)

while True:
    for i in range(n):
        np[i] = (100,100,100)
        np.show() 
        sleep(100)
        np.clear()

children.text: In Basics
you have already access to the most frequently used type of loops, the
while loop
In while loops, the program continues repeating an action until the condition becomes false.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import speech

count = 0
while count < 5:
    display.scroll(count)
    count = count + 1
speech.say('five')

children.text: For instance, in this code, the loop runs until the count variable reaches 5.
When the count reaches 5, the loop stops, and the program executes the line outside the loop, saying 'five' only once.
This concludes the loop.
This will scroll ‘Emma’ on the display 2 times:
The range() function begins counting at 0 by default and stops just before the specified end of the range. Therefore, when used in a loop such as
for i in range(5):
, it will iterate over the numbers from 0 to 4, causing the loop to execute 5 times.
You can specify the starting number for the
range()
function. Here's an example in Python:
This counts from 0 to 10 in steps of 2, showing the counting values: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
The
range()
function starts at 5 and stops just before 0. This loop counts down from 5 to 1 in steps of -1:
Utilize '
for
' loops to iterate through items in a
list

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

names = ["Emma", "Lucca", "Charlie", "Lee"]

for name in names:
    display.scroll(name)
    sleep(1000)

children.text: In this example, the list of words is stored in the variable
names
. The for loop is used to call up all the words one after the other.
For
' loops can iterate over each character within a string.

content.main:
from microbit import *

for char in 'Emma':
    display.show(char)
    sleep(1000)

children.text: In this case,
char
is used as the variable name to represent each character in the string. You can use any valid variable name of your choice to achieve the same result.
Count-controlled loops, referred to as '
for
' loops, iterate over sections of code for a specified number of iterations.
It's possible to place loops inside other loops, which is called "nesting" loops.
This example lights up the LED display one pixel at a time, going through the rows (y) and, inside each row, through the columns (x).
You can exit a loop using
break
In this example the looping of the animation "Press A to break" stops if button A is pressed as the program breaks out of the loop when the event happens.
This code scrolls the message "Press A to break" on the Calliope mini's display until button A is pressed, at which point it exits the loop and displays "Done".
Python uses
indentation
to tell the computer exactly which statements to execute, similar to how it uses indentation to indicate which lines of code are in a loop.

contents.name: if, elif, else
compatibility: Python uses indentation to tell the computer exactly which statements to execute, similar to how it uses indentation to indicate which lines of code are in a loop.

children.text: Use
if
to test if something is true:
The code checks if the A-button is pressed and displays “A” if it is.
elif
is an abbreviation for
else if
. Employ it to introduce an additional condition to your if statement.
This checks if the A button is pressed and displays an A if so. If the A button is not pressed, the code then checks if the B button is pressed and displays “B”.
Include 'else' to account for any other scenarios:
If neither A nor B is pressed, “X” is displayed.
You can compare numbers to make different things happen if they are equal, smaller, larger or not equal to something.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

score = 5
if score == 5:
    display.scroll('It's a tie!')

from calliopemini import *

score = 4
if score < 5:
    display.scroll('You lost the game!')

from calliopemini import *


number = 6
if number > 5:
    display.scroll('You won the game!')

from calliopemini import *


score = 5
if score <= 5:
    display.scroll('Your score is less than or equal to 5!')

from calliopemini import *


score = 5
if score >= 5:
    display.scroll('Your score is greater than or equal to 5!')

from calliopemini import *


score = 12
if score != 5:
    display.scroll('Your score does not match 5!')

children.text: You can combine conditions using logical operators like
and
or
and
not.
The
and
operator, also called junction combines two conditions. If both are true the code below is executed:
The
or
operator, also called disjunction, combines two conditions. If either condition is true, the code below is executed.
The
not
operator, also known as negation, changes the condition to its opposite. If the original condition is true, "not" makes it false, and vice versa.
Each time we press button A, we check the temperature. If it's warm, we show a happy face; if it's not warm, we show a sad face.
You can put
if
statements inside each other. This is called ‘nesting’.
Conditional booleans help us make decisions in code. They're like switches that can either be "on" or "off" depending on a certain condition.
This program essentially reacts to the amount of light detected by the Calliope mini. If it's dark, it shows a sad face; if there's enough light, it shows a happy face.
You can break out of a
loop
using conditional statements and
break

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

counter = 0

while True:
    counter += 1
    if accelerometer.was_gesture("shake"):
        break

display.show(counter)

children.text: This code keeps counting until the Calliope mini is shaken. Once it feels a shake, it stops counting and shows the total number of shakes on the display.
Variables can be assigned with the equal sign
Initialize variables to their starting values at the beginning of a program using the equal sign:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

my_age = 20
print("I am", my_age, "years old.")

children.text: Boolean variables can only be
True
or
False
and are useful for controlling your program.
A collection of words or symbols is referred to as a string. Enclose the contents of a string within quotation marks:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

text = 'Calliope mini'
display.scroll(text)

children.text: To initialize variables for the first time, they should be declared at the top of the code or at the start of the program.
Variable names should have the following characteristics:

Variable names should describe what they're used for to make the code easy to understand. 
For example, Boolean variables describe states, such as "is_raining", and numbers are named according to what they represent, such as "apples" or "time".
Names must start with a letter, not a number, and they can't have spaces.
Also, they can't be the same as special words that Python uses, like "True" or "if".
Remember, variables in Python are case-sensitive, so "number" and "Number" would be considered different variables.
Generally variables can be overwritten by reassigning them in the code. Variables do not need to be declared with any particular
type
, and can even change type after they have been set.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
x = "12"
display.scroll(x)

x = "Caro"
display.scroll(x)

children.text: Numeric variables can be changed by performing addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division operations.
Use
to increase, or increment, the value of a variable:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *


number = 3
number += 5
display.scroll(number)

children.text: This augments the value of the variable
number
by 10, resulting in a display of 13. It achieves the same effect as
number = number + 10
, but it is more concise and easier to type.
Utilize
to decrease or decrement the value of a variable.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *


number = 8
number -= 3
display.scroll(number)

children.text: This reduces the value of the variable
number
by 3, resulting in a display of 5. It is equivalent to the operation
number = number - 3
Use
to multiply the value of a variable:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
number = 5
number *= 10
display.scroll(number)

children.text: This example multiplies the value of the variable
number
by 10, resulting in a display of 50. It is equivalent to the operation
number = number * 10
Utilize
to divide the value of a variable.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *


number = 9
number /= 2
display.scroll(number)

children.text: This example divides the value of the variable
number
by 3, resulting in a display of 3.0. It is equivalent to the operation
number = number / 3
The datatypes of variables can be changed among strings, floats, and numbers. This can be done by "casting":

content.main:
x = str(5)    # x will be '5'
y = int(5)    # y will be 5
z = float(5)  # z will be 5.0

children.text: Some functions with specified data types will throw an error. For example, if you try to perform a math operation with text. That's where casting variables comes in handy.

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
string = "4"
result = int(string) + 3

children.text: In Python,
global variables
are defined outside of any function and can be accessed from anywhere within the program. They maintain their value throughout the entire program execution. In contrast,
local variables
are defined within a function and can only be accessed within that function's scope. They are temporary and exist only as long as the function is executing.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

global_var = 10
def function_with_local_var():
    local_var = 5
    display.scroll(str(local_var))

display.scroll(str(global_var))
function_with_local_var()

contents.name: Variables
contents.subtitle: Store and change data for usage.

children.text: Variables serve the purpose of storing data that can change.
For advanced mathmatical operations the math library needs to exported at the beginning:
math import *

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

calc = 10 + 5
display.scroll(calc)

children.text: Addition

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

calc = 10 - 5
display.scroll(calc)

from calliopemini import *

calc = 10 * 5
display.scroll(calc)

from calliopemini import *

calc = 10 / 5
display.scroll(calc)

from calliopemini import *

calc = 2 ** 5
display.scroll(calc)

children.text: This operation will raise the base number 2 to the power of 5, resulting in the value 32.
The modulo shows the remainder of a number when divided.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

calc = 20 % 7 
display.scroll(calc)

children.text: In this example, the code calculates the remainder when dividing 20 by 7. The remainder is 6, because 20 / 7 = 2 and the rest of it 20 -  2 * 7 = 6.
The
operator divides two numbers and always rounds down the result:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
calc = 11 // 6
display.scroll(calc)

children.text: The result of dividing 11 by 6 is 1.833333, but the variable
calc
holds the value 1 because it rounds down.

Floor division behaves opposite to the modulo. While the modulo operator % provides the remainder of a number as a whole number (integer) when divided, floor division yields the quotient as a whole number, excluding the remainder.
In Python, mathematical operations do not follow a left-to-right evaluation; instead, certain operations are prioritized over others. The order of calculations is as follows:
Brackets (parentheses)
Exponentials (raise to the power of)
Multiplication
, division
, modulo (remainder)
, floor division
Addition
and subtraction

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *

display.scroll(2 + 2 * 5)
display.scroll((2 + 2) * 10)

children.text: In this Python example, the first displayed number is 12, as multiplication takes precedence over addition. The second displayed number, 40, is obtained by first adding 2 and 2, then multiplying the result by 10.
You need to include
import random
to the beginning of your program.
This example will display a random integers between 0 and 10.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import random

random_integer = random.randint(0, 10)
display.show(random_integer)

children.text: This example will display a floating number between 2 and 4.

content.main:
import random 

random_float = random.uniform(2, 4) 
display.scroll(random_float)

children.text: This example will generate a random boolean value, that is either
True
or
False
Use also
random.choice(

) to select a random item or word from a list.
See
Lists
to learn more about how to make use of lists in Python.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import random

colors = ['red', 'green', 'blue', 'yellow']

while True:
    if button_a.is_pressed():
        chosen_color = random.choice(colors)
        display.show(chosen_color)
        sleep(1000)
        display.clear()

children.text: The
abs()
function converts a number, regardless of its sign (positive or negative), to its absolute (positive) value.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

number = -5
display.scroll("Original: {}".format(number))
absolute_value = abs(number)
display.scroll("Absolute: {}".format(absolute_value))

children.text: Numbers can be rounded up or down, to integers and decimal places.
Utilize the
int()
function to convert a decimal (floating-point) number into a whole number (integer). It rounds down. The displayed result in this example is 5.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
display.scroll(int(5.5))

children.text: The
round()
function is designed to round numbers to a specified number of decimal places. When no decimal places are specified, it defaults to rounding to a whole number.
For instance, applying
will round the number to three decimal places, displaying 5.234 on the LED display:

content.main: display.scroll(round(5.2342,3))

children.text: Employ
floor()
to round down. Ensure you include
from math import floor
near the beginning of your program. This will round 5.7 down to 5.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import floor 
 
display.scroll(floor(5.7))

children.text: Utilize
ceil()
to round up. Be sure to include
from math import ceil
near the start of your program. This will round 4.1 up to 5:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import ceil 
 
display.scroll(ceil(4.1))

children.text: Trigonometric functions such as sine, cosine, and tangent represent ratios of sides in a right-angled triangle and accept values in radians, which are measured using π (
p
i), a constant approximately equal to 3.141593. In Python,
pi
can be used as a constant:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import *

display.scroll(pi)

from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(cos(1))

from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(sin(1))

from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(tan(1))

from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(acos(1))

from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(asin(1))

from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(atan(1))

from calliopemini import *
from math import *

display.scroll(atan2(1,1))

children.text: Radians can be converted to degrees and vice versa:

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import *

display.scroll(radians(180))
display.scroll(degrees(pi))

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import * 

display.scroll(math.pow(2, 2))

children.text: The alternative notation with the
operator can also be used to exponentiate one number with another:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import * 

display.scroll(2 ** 2)

from calliopemini import *
from math import *

display.scroll(e)

children.text: Euler's number,
, is displayed on the screen.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import *

display.scroll(log(10))

children.text: With one argument, this will return the natural logarithm of 10 to base
e
With 2 arguents this will show 10 to base 2:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(log(10, 2))

children.text: Return the square root of 9, which is 3.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
from math import *


display.scroll(sqrt(9))

children.text: Before utilizing the radio, ensure that you activate it.

content.main:
import radio


radio.on()

children.text: As the radio feature consumes more power, it may be advisable to deactivate it during specific intervals to conserve battery life:

detailContent.main:
import radio


radio.off()

children.text: Initially, establish a radio group to ensure that your message is directed to the appropriate Calliope mini or group of Calliope mini.

content.main:
import radio

radio.config(group=12)

children.text: All Calliope mini within the same group number can exchange radio messages.
Any group number ranging from 0 to 255 can be utilized.
You have the option to transmit strings composed of letters, symbols, and numbers over the radio.

content.main:
import radio


radio.on()
radio.send('Calliope mini')
radio.off()

children.text: Due to the unpredictable timing of radio message transmissions, it is recommended to continuously monitor for new messages within a loop. This strategy guarantees the prompt display of newly received messages (information) as soon as they arrive.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import radio

radio.on()
while True:
    info = radio.receive()
    if info:
        display.scroll(info)

children.text: Optionally, you can set the radio transmit power within a range from 0 to 7:

content.main:
import radio

radio.config(group=12, power=5)

children.text: Setting the power to 0 means the lowest power, and 7 means the highest. Using higher power makes radio signals go further, but it uses up more battery. Changing the power setting might help the battery last longer.
With the integrated motor driver, two motors can be moved independently of each other.
Motor 0 runs forward at full speed:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_DIR.write_digital(0)
pin_M0_SPEED.write_analog(1023)

children.text: Motor 1 runs backwards at full speed:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M1_DIR.write_digital(1)
pin_M1_SPEED.write_analog(1023)

children.text: Motor 0 is actively braked, i.e. the speed of the motor is set to 0:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_DIR.write_digital(1)
pin_M0_SPEED.write_analog(0)

children.text: With the
pin_M0_DIR
for motor 0 and
pin_M1_DIR
for motor 1 the running direction can be defined. If the value of the pin is set to 1, then the motor runs backward and with 0 correspondingly forward.
The speed is set by the analog pin
pin_M0_SPEED
, respectively
pin_M1_SPEED
for motor 1. 1023 is full speed and 0 active braking.
Two motors run forward at full speed:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_DIR.write_digital(0)
pin_M1_DIR.write_digital(0)

pin_M0_SPEED.write_analog(1023)
pin_M1_SPEED.write_analog(1023)

children.text: Zwei Motoren laufen bei der vollen Geschwindigkeit rückwärts:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_DIR.write_digital(1)
pin_M1_DIR.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_SPEED.write_analog(1023)
pin_M1_SPEED.write_analog(1023)

children.text: If one motor is braked or runs slower than the other, then steering is possible:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_DIR.write_digital(1)
pin_M1_DIR.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_SPEED.write_analog(0)
pin_M1_SPEED.write_analog(1023)

children.text: If one motor is braked or runs slower than the other, then steering is possible:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_DIR.write_digital(1)
pin_M1_DIR.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_SPEED.write_analog(1023)
pin_M1_SPEED.write_analog(0)

children.text: Set the analog pins of both motors to 0 to stop:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

pin_M_MODE.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_DIR.write_digital(1)
pin_M1_DIR.write_digital(1)

pin_M0_SPEED.write_analog(0)
pin_M1_SPEED.write_analog(0)

children.text: With the
pin_M0_DIR
for motor 0 and
pin_M1_DIR
for motor 1 the running direction can be defined. If the value of the pin is set to 0, then the motor runs counterclockwise and with 1 correspondingly clockwise.
The speed is set by the analog pin
pin_M0_SPEED
, resp.
pin_M1_SPEED
for motor 1. 1023 is full speed and 0 active braking.
Two motors can thus be controlled independently of each other and thus a vehicle can be steered, for example.

contents.name: Motors
contents.subtitle: Control one or two motors with the Calliope mini

children.text: Functions in Python are like recipes in cooking. They are blocks of code that you can reuse whenever you need them. You can give them inputs (ingredients) and they will give you outputs (dishes) based on those inputs.
Procedures are functions designed to execute a predetermined set of instructions. With
def
functions can be named and defined once in the program:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

def blinking_heart():
    for i in range(3):
        display.show(Image.HEART)
        sleep(500)
        display.clear()
        sleep(500)


blinking_heart()

children.text: The blinking_heart() function blinks a heart for 3 times. You can call the function by writing it down below your definition, otherwise it will throw an error. If you call it twice, the heart will blink 6 times.
Functions can have inputs (parameters) to customize their behavior. The input is defined as a local variable inside the brackets of the function.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

def blinking_heart(times, delay=1000):
    for i in range(times):
        display.show(Image.HEART)
        sleep(delay/2)
        display.clear()
        sleep(delay/2)

children.text: Displays the specified image on the Calliope mini's LED display and waits for a custom duration.
Used parameters:
image_to_display (Image):
Defines the image to be displayed.  The duration to wait is defined with
custom_delay (int)
, in milliseconds. Defaults to 1000 milliseconds (1 second).

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *

def display_custom_image_with_delay(custom_image, custom_delay=2000):
    display.show(custom_image)
    sleep(custom_delay)
display_custom_image_with_delay(Image.SMILE)
display_custom_image_with_delay(Image.SAD, custom_delay=4000)
display.clear()

children.text: The function
is_dark()
checks if the light level is below 50 on the Calliope mini, returning
True
if it is and
False
otherwise.
Functions in Python can return various data types, including booleans, numbers, and strings, which can then be used as inputs for other functions.
Functions can process information and
return
it.

contents.name: Functions
contents.subtitle: Use functions to structure and maintain your program

children.text: Name your lists just like variables. Enclose list elements in square brackets, separated by commas.

content.main: fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'orange']

children.text: Strings must be enclosed in quotation marks.
Accessing elements in lists employs numerical indices, with the first item starting at 0. Consequently, displaying the first item on the screen would involve scrolling 'Apple.'

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
 
fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Orange', 3]
display.scroll(fruits[0])

children.text: Iterate through all elements of a list sequentially by employing a 'for' loop:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
 
 
fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Orange', 3]
for item in fruits:
    display.scroll(item)

children.text: Incorporate the
random
module for access to
random.choice()
, facilitating the retrieval of a random element from a list.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import random

fruits = ["I like apples!", "I like bananas!", "I like oranges!"]

while True:
    display.scroll(random.choice(fruits))
    sleep(2000)

children.text: This program imports the necessary modules, defines a list of messages, and then continuously displays a randomly chosen message on the LED display of the Calliope mini, scrolling the message across. The
random.choice()
function is used to pick a random element from the list.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import random

favouredfruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Orange']
display.scroll(random.choice(favouredfruits))

children.text: This action will substitute the element at index 1 with the integer 1.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *


fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 2]
fruits[1] = 1

children.text: Utilize the insert method to add elements at a specified position in a list:

content.main:
fruits = ['Apple', 'Kiwi', 'Oranges']
letters.insert(1,'Banana')

children.text: Insert the word 'Banana' at index 1, representing the second item in the list when counting from 0.
Items can be deleted by their position in the list using
pop()

content.main:
fruits = ['Apple', 'Kiwi', 'Banana', 'Orange']
fruits.pop(1)

children.text: This removes the item located at index 1, so it deletes ‘Kiwi’, from the list.
Utilize
remove()
to eliminate an element from a list based on its value rather than its position:

content.main:
fruits = ['Apple', 'Kiwi', 'Banana', 'Orange']
fruits.remove('Kiwi')

children.text: This operation will remove 'Kiwi' from any position in the list.
Utilize
clear()
to remove all elements from a list:

content.main:
fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Kiwi', 'Orange']
fruits.clear()

children.text: Employ the
sort()
method to alphabetically sort lists:

content.main:
fruits = ['Orange', 'Kiwi', 'Apple', 'Banana']
fruits.sort()

children.text: Utilize
reverse()
to invert the order of a selected list:

content.main:
fruits = ['Orange', 'Kiwi', 'Banana', 'Apple']
fruits.reverse()

children.text: Lists containing various data types can be reversed, but for alphabetical or numerical sorting, the list must consist entirely of the same data type. For instance, all elements should be either strings or integers.
Utilize
len()
to determine the length of a list:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Kiwi']
display.scroll(len(fruits))

children.text: This shows a 3 on the LED display because there are 3 elements in the list.
Employ
count()
to tally the occurrences of a specific element in a list:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

fruits = ['Apple', 'Apple', 'Banana', 'Kiwi', 'Orange']
display.scroll(fruits.count('Apple'))

children.text: This displays 2 because
Apple
occurs twice in the list.

contents.name: Lists
contents.subtitle: Create lists to structure your data efficiently.

contents.name: Data recording
contents.subtitle: Record sensor information on your Calliope mini.

children.text: This example will create three column headings titled
X
Y
and Temp.
The first column in your log holds the timestamp and will be added to every row of data. You can set the format of the timestamp when you set your column labels to
MILLISECONDS
SECONDS
MINUTES
HOURS
DAYS
or
NONE
if you want to disable the timestamp.
This example sets the format to record the time in  'seconds':

detailContent.main:
import log 

log.set_labels('X', 'Y', 'Temp', timestamp=log.SECONDS)

children.text: For the data logging setup, provide descriptions for your data, which will serve as the column headings.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import log

log.set_labels('X', 'Y', 'Temp')

children.text: The example above adds an entry to the
X
Y
and
Temp
columns using values from the
accelerometer
and
temperature sensor
The titles and corresponding values are supplied to
log.add()
through a dictionary.
A dictionary is a data structure composed of key:value pairs enclosed in curly brackets {}. Each entry includes a label and its associated value.
Instead of employing dictionary values, an alternative method is to use keyword arguments with
log.add()
. The following example logs the same data:

detailContent.main:
from calliopemini import *
import log


log.add(
    X: accelerometer.get_x(),
    Y: accelerometer.get_y(),
    Temp=temperature()
)

children.text: You have the capability to log data from any of the built-in sensors on your Calliope mini:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import log


log.add({
  'X': accelerometer.get_x(),
  'Y': accelerometer.get_y(),
  'Temp': temperature()
})

children.text: A scheduler placed before the
log_data()
function can log the data at specified intervals:
In this examples the data is recorded every minute.
Every other time unit parameter can be used as well:
@run_every(h=1, min=15, s=30, ms=100)
would log data every 1 hour, 15 minutes, 30 seconds, and 100 milliseconds.
The while loop is necessary to keep the program running, while the scheduler will call every given interval the function
log_data().
Use the
print()
function to output text or numbers to the serial console:

content.main:
from calliopemini import *

while True:
    temperature = temperature()
    print("Temperature: {}C".format(temperature))
    sleep(1000)

children.text: In this example, the current temperature is printed every second.
This is helpful for finding and fixing problems in a program or checking sensor readings in a particular situation.

contents.name: Print output to the serial console

children.text: Interact with your programs by inputting text using your computer keyboard.

content.main:
from calliopemini import *
import random

secret_number = random.randint(1, 10)
guess = int(input('Guess the secret number (between 1 and 10): '))
if guess == secret_number:
    print('Congratulations! You guessed the secret number.')
    display.scroll(secret_number)
else:
    print('Oops! The secret number was {}. Better luck next time.'.format(secret_number))
    display.scroll(secret_number)

children.text: This example introduces a guessing game where the user interacts by entering their guess using the computer's keyboard. The result is shown within the editor and on the Calliope mini. It's a fun way to explore input and conditional statements.
REPL stands for Read Evaluate Print Loop: the Calliope mini reads your instruction, evaluates it, then prints the result in the serial console.
Having connected your Calliope mini and flashed a Python program to it, break out of the program by pressing crtl+C to access the command prompt
Type
help()
to get some ideas about what you can do.
You can use the serial console to type and execute Python commands directly on your Calliope mini.

contents.name: Serial communication
contents.subtitle: Print text to the console or interact with your program through serial communication.

children.text: Serial communication allows you to exchange information with other devices, such as the Calliope mini with your computer. If you're using a browser like Chrome or Edge, you can directly output the information to the integrated console.
Then console pops up at the bottom of your editor, when you have connected the calliope mini with an USB-cable to your computer:

description: Explore with Python the features of your Calliope mini
